questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Being in a convenient location in SE Asia with easy access to neighbouring countries for travel as well as being a highly ranked university, so i expected a high quality education. Singapore is also a very unique country as it has prospered under a rule which we might consider autocratic in Denmark, which is interesting to explore as an economist.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Mails are being sent frequently to keep you in the loop. Going on exchange to a non-EU country is pretty troublesome no matter where you go, so expect a pretty large amount of paperwork. Download whatsapp/telegram as thats what people use over there for social as well as academic matters.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had a question about check-in which i posed in the NUS-Exchangers whatsapp group, and another exchanger helped me out. Other than that the documents i was sent by email were sufficient.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: You can stay in Halls which are dorms with a shared kitchen, Residential colleges which are somewhat similar i think, i didnt live in those. The clear best choice imo is UTown Residence with airconditioning. It has an amazing location on campus, and you get an apartment with 3 others (i was with 3 exchangers) with aircon - VERY important - and a little kitchen area/living room.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Halls and RCs have meal plans, UTown Residence kitchen only has a microwave, no stove or oven. It's fine though, as the culture in SG is to eat at food courts (also known as hawker centres) for lunch and dinner, which is very affordable. A typical lunch/dinner is 5sgd or 25dkk.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Definitely go for an option with aircon. Besides Utown residence, PGP has some, i cant speak to what its like living there though. I think some RCs have aswell, which might be a good choice too. Halls and RCs got a lot of activities going on, and its definitely easier to make local friends that way, so there's a tradeoff to have in mind between comfort/privacy and the sweaty and social Hall experience

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You get emails about the registration dates. I got all 4 of my first priority courses in the first round, but 1 of them got cancelled for some reason. I got the next best course in the second round.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can email the uni about course registration and have assistance if you need that.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all i wanted with no issues.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Theres a period of 3-4 weeks iirc at the start of the semester where you can freely drop courses. So just sign up for too many courses and go to 1-2 lectures/classes and sort it out from there.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The course selection as an economy student is very limited as an exchanger. I could choose between something like 7-8 courses, despite the university offering 30-40 appropriate for a 3rd year student. Very frustrating.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses are generally low. In Money and Banking and Financial Economics half the course was about Time Value of Money, which was covered in the first semester at KU. They also didn't want us to do lagrange for optimization problems in one course, as "that might be too advanced for the exchange students"?? Game Theory was taught by an Oxford professor and was more like the level of KU. Urban economics is very conceptually interesting, it is however not very difficult either, which can also be seen as an upside of course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Lectures are like at home. However tutorials are a complete sham. Each course had 1 hour each week for tutorial, which had the following program: Students solve weekly tutorial sheet at home, students volunteer or a picked to present a question at the whiteboard, the class sits in silence for 7 minutes while the students at the whiteboard painstakingly write every step of the derivations as they are graded on their tutorial contribution, they quickly talk through their work.  Rinse and repeat for next questions, class dismissed.

Grading is not based on 1 exam like it is at home. Final exam is 40-60% of your grade, and most courses have midterms which are 15-30%. Rest are canvas quizzes (literally free grade since you can take them multiple times) and tutorial participation and attendance. Attendance is mandatory, but you can skip a few times during the semester without any repercussions. I cannot overstate enough how lenient the grading is too. Passing is basically expected no matter what you do, and with minimal effort you can get a comfortable B.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Urban Economics, Money and Banking, Financial Economics, Game Theory and Applications to Economics.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Game Theory and Applications to Economics to get Mikro 3 merit, Urban Economics because it's unlike anything we have at KU and super interesting imo, by far my favorite course there. Financial Economics gives merit as a "prioriteret valgfag" so that might also be important to you. Money and Banking was easy and not my field of interest, ymmv.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Alcohol is very expensive, eating out is very inexpensive. I traveled a lot (went to 8 countries during and after the exchange), so naturally there was quite a bit of "personal spending". Housing was cheaper than my apartment at home.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They've got loads of sports and halls with all kinds of activities going on. Big olympic pool and squash courts etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the arrangements and outings people do in the Whatsapp group, easy to make some friends that way, everybody got 0 friends at first. Your housing place most likely has an orientation week as well, go to those events and get to know the people in your building, you'll be seeing them every day!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore the city, travel around asia. I selected my courses and tutorial times so they were all on mon/tue so i had 5 day weekend each week. NUSMods has a tool that allows you to import the course and make your schedule that way. Also go to China, they made it visa-free for Danes in November 2024, and it's so fun to go there and speak to local and get a feel for the country by yourself. Ask about the political and economic situation if you befriend a local, they arent all as shy as we think.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I was in a bit of an exchanger bubble, but Singapore is very orderly and distinctly different from the rest of SE Asia. It's not hard to adjust at all. Most people speak english too.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Theres a buddy programme you can sign up for before the exchange starts, many exchangers did so and had good experiences. Talking to people in your classes is good too, you've already got a shared interest! (or disinterest).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Understanding what the mandarin speaking ladies at some of the food stands were yelling at me.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: They do a lot of "raising" the society to have proper manners, lots of campaign ads to not harass the bus driver and to give your seat to old people and pregnant woman etc. They are also way ahead of their time in many urban policies, such as having a congestion tax since the 1980's, which is now slowly being introduced in western and chinese large cities. Their research and knowledge in urban policy in general is very advanced, go to NUS Cities events if that sort of thing interests you.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: DO NOT GET SINGTEL AS YOUR TELECOM PROVIDER 3x. Get an E-sim from someone else if you can, or something like the 200GB local data and 7GB roaming abroad from Simba (60dkk/month). Have fun :)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think i covered most of it in the previous sections.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Finding interests in new economic fields, forging strong bonds, expanding my worldview to different forms of government and having a lot of fun while doing it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: There's a lot of work to do before going, by keeping up with the whole process, seeking forhåndsgodkendelse and selecting courses and housing, seeking grants (legater), subletting your accomodation in Denmark and so on.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: NUS is an amazing place to go, and you can have an unforgettable semester there. I think that's the case in most places though, so wherever you end up going, being curious and social is the key to making your exchange the best it can be.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
